The episode happened Monday afternoon at the Six Flags Over Georgia amusement park, the police said. It was not immediately clear what led up to the rider’s death.

Listen

![Image 1: An aerial view of a park worker in a yellow shirt helping riders evacuate a roller coaster.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/12/multimedia/12xp-roller-coaster-1/12xp-roller-coaster-1-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

An image from a video shows a park worker helping riders evacuate a roller coaster after a rider died at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday.Credit...11alive

Oct. 12, 2026 Updated 8:43 p.m. ET

One rider died and several others were injured on Monday on a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, the police said.

The Cobb County Police Department said in a statement that the episode happened at 3:58 p.m. at the amusement park in Austell, Ga., about 17 miles west of Atlanta.

Details about how the rider died, as well as the number of people injured and their conditions, were not immediately available.

A Six Flags representative said in a statement that park officials and the local authorities had responded immediately, but declined to describe what happened, citing the family’s privacy.

“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the representative said. “Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends and loved ones.”

The representative also declined to say which roller coaster was involved.

The episode on Monday happened less than a month after [three people sued Six Flags and S&S Worldwide](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/23/us/six-flags-x2-roller-coaster-injuries.html?eafs_enabled=false), a manufacturer of roller coaster vehicles, saying they suffered catastrophic brain injuries after riding X2, a roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain amusement park in Southern California.

The lawsuits accused Six Flags of failing to adequately warn passengers about the risks to riders.

The X2 is a 200-foot-high roller coaster with seats that rotate independently as the train travels along the track, spinning riders by as much as [360 degrees](https://www.sixflags.com/magicmountain/attractions/x2-coaster). It reaches speeds of up to [76 miles an hour](https://www.sixflags.com/blog/thrill-roller-coaster-guide-to-six-flags-magic-mountain) and sends riders through dives, flips and twists.

In court filings in an earlier case involving X2, Six Flags denied that the roller coaster had caused a rider’s fatal brain injury. The ride has been closed since July.

Christina Morales contributed reporting.

_This is a developing story. Check back for updates._

## America’s Favorite Fruit Is Being Bruised by the Iran War

The journey of one banana from farm to store shows how the war’s economic effects have cascaded into some surprising industries.

Transporting bananas to the United States has become much trickier since the war in Iran put pressure on global supply chains.Credit...Hannah Beier for The New York Times

Listen

· 10:19 min

Oct. 12, 2026 Updated 1:36 p.m. ET

The war in Iran has rippled through the global economy in many ways, pushing up prices for oil, fertilizer and other products. It has also created challenges for America’s most popular fruit: bananas.

The banana business has long been an underappreciated feat of logistics. It involves transporting a fragile and finicky fruit thousands of miles from the tropics, only to be sold for less than a quarter each. And it’s a business that is even trickier of late as the war raises the costs of fuel and other materials banana producers need.

That has put even more financial pressure on banana producers, who operate with thin margins and have little ability to raise prices. Compounding the industry’s problems are the threat of disease, climate change, tariffs and an exceptionally severe El Niño this year.

The banana might be America’s most unassuming fruit, a cheaply priced staple of smoothies and school cafeterias. It is the most consumed fruit in the United States, with Americans eating around 80 bananas a year, on average.

But bananas make little profit for grocery stores or the companies growing them. Instead, stores price them cheaply to draw shoppers in the door. The average price of bananas in the United States — about 65 cents a pound in August — [has changed little](https://www.bls.gov/charts/consumer-price-index/consumer-price-index-average-price-data.htm) over the last decade, despite rising costs.

“Everything is costing more money,” said Danny Dumas, a senior vice president at Del Monte North America. “If you ask me, it is a crisis.”

items.title: A Contagious Aversion to Overhead Lights
items.summary: Plus: How far to go for a colleague, and now your chance to give someone advice.
items.full_text: Send questions about the office, money, careers and work-life balance to workfriend@nytimes.com . Include your name and location, or a request to remain anonymous. Letters may be edited. Dear Work Friend, I manage a team of about 20 people in an open-plan office suite. A few months ago, one of my staff members asked that we disconnect the overhead lighting above his pod because he is prone to migraines. His co-workers didn’t object, so I complied. That corner of the office is now permanently dark, which isn’t ideal, but I’ve been willing to tolerate it. Last week, a worker in another corner of the office asked to work from home in the morning because her husband’s schedule had changed and she needed to be home to care for her two preschoolers. I said she could change her schedule if necessary, but not work from home while also caring for a 2- and 4-year-old. She escalated to the union, but the union supported my decision. Yesterday, she came back with a request to have the lights above her desk disconnected as well, saying she also suffers from migraines. Today, a third employee, a close friend of the second, said that she, too, suffers migraines and needs the lights disabled. This feels like a retaliatory protest, and obviously, I cannot agree to the entire office being plunged into a perpetual state of gloom with no overhead lights. My question is, in declining the two new requests, should I then also revert to full lighting for the whole office? That feels like penalizing a person with a legitimate health need for two disgruntled staffers. — Anonymous This is an interesting letter, because I’m not sure the advice you need is the advice you’re looking for. The answer to your specific question is pretty obvious: No, you should not revert to full lighting for the whole office. Your migraine-suffering employee’s accommodation was made separately from these two later (and, to your mind, suspicious) requests. Right now you have two apparently disgruntled employees; why would you add a third? I understand why you’re looking to assert some authority here. You’re afraid of being undermined by employee rebellion. (And afraid of a darkened office.) But being a manager isn’t solely about maintaining dispensatory power, and flexibility and creativity can often defuse tension more effectively than a rigid commitment to particular rules — or, for that matter, to particular office lighting schemes. Rather than roll back accommodations for the sake of fairness (or to make a point), I would at least consider trying to meet your other employees halfway. For all you know, their requests are legitimate and the connection to the contentious schedule change is coincidental. (“Bad migraines” doesn’t seem like a far-fetched condition for a woman with two young kids and a stressful schedule.) Could you, for example, move the two newly incapacitated employees to the same darker section of the office as the original migraine sufferer? This might blunt their frustration, and even earn some good will, without darkening the entire office. Or you might go in one day this week and try to look at the office lighting as lighting rather than as leverage. Is a less brightly lit office really “gloomy”? Is that one corner “permanently dark,” or naturally — even soothingly — lit? Would individual desk lamps be better for everyone? Is it possible that the migraine sufferers have a point? You could even consult some of the other employees to see how they feel. Some of them may hate the darkness as much as you do, which would at least give you more ground to stand on in rejecting the newer requests. These exercises may amount to nothing; creativity is not a panacea. And it’s true, you’re backed into a (particularly ill-lit) corner right now because you made the original accommodation informally. But the best alternative to casual flexibility is a formal, neutral and transparent process, not arbitrary rollbacks. In other words, if you can’t absorb tension through creative management, absorb it into bureaucracy.
